claim: Ongoing brain oscillations are known to influence perception.
source: Ongoing brain oscillations are known to influence perception, and to be reset by exogenous stimulations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research showing the relationship between brain oscillations and perception.

claim: Ongoing brain oscillations are reset by exogenous stimulations.
source: Ongoing brain oscillations are known to influence perception, and to be reset by exogenous stimulations.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on oscillatory reset by external stimuli.

claim: Voluntary action is accompanied by prominent rhythmic activity.
source: Voluntary action is also accompanied by prominent rhythmic activity, and recent behavioral evidence suggests that this might be coupled with perception.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research on rhythmic activity during voluntary action.

claim: Recent behavioral evidence suggests that rhythmic activity during voluntary action might be coupled with perception.
source: Voluntary action is also accompanied by prominent rhythmic activity, and recent behavioral evidence suggests that this might be coupled with perception.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior behavioral studies.

claim: The phase of theta oscillations (~4 Hz) predicts perceptual performance.
source: The phase of theta oscillations (~4 Hz) predicts perceptual performance, even >1 s before movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data from the EEG and behavioral experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: The phase of theta oscillations predicts perceptual performance even more than 1 second before movement.
source: The phase of theta oscillations (~4 Hz) predicts perceptual performance, even >1 s before movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing early predictive effects at approximately -1.4 s.

claim: Theta oscillations are phase-locked to the onset of the movement.
source: Moreover, theta oscillations are phase-locked to the onset of the movement.
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data showing phase-locking to movement onset.

claim: The alignment of theta phase and its perceptual relevance unfold with similar non-monotonic profiles.
source: Remarkably, the alignment of theta phase and its perceptual relevance unfold with similar non-monotonic profiles, suggesting their relatedness.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing matching temporal profiles in Figures 3a and 3d.

claim: The similar non-monotonic profiles of theta phase alignment and perceptual relevance suggest their relatedness.
source: Remarkably, the alignment of theta phase and its perceptual relevance unfold with similar non-monotonic profiles, suggesting their relatedness.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the observed similarity in temporal profiles.

claim: Perception and movement initiation are automatically synchronized since the early stages of motor planning through neuronal oscillatory activity in the theta range.
source: The present work shows that perception and movement initiation are automatically synchronized since the early stages of motor planning through neuronal oscillatory activity in the theta range.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data showing theta phase effects on perception during motor preparation.

claim: Low-level visual function is rhythmically modulated during preparation for a voluntary movement of the arm.
source: We recently provided behavioral evidence that low-level visual function is rhythmically modulated during preparation for a voluntary movement of the arm (Tomassini et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: Theta-band fluctuations of visual contrast sensitivity are time-locked to the movement and emerge before its onset.
source: In fact, we found theta-band fluctuations of visual contrast sensitivity that are time-locked to the movement and emerge before its onset.
evidence: This is supported by citation to prior work by the authors.

claim: The rhythmic modulation of visual function during motor preparation affects visual stimuli that are unrelated to the motor task.
source: Crucially, this modulation affects visual stimuli that are unrelated to the motor task (Tomassini et al., 2015; Benedetto et al., 2016), extending traditional notions of the corollary discharge (Crapse and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The modulation of visual stimuli unrelated to the motor task extends traditional notions of the corollary discharge.
source: Crucially, this modulation affects visual stimuli that are unrelated to the motor task (Tomassini et al., 2015; Benedetto et al., 2016), extending traditional notions of the corollary discharge (Crapse and Sommer, 2008).
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited findings and comparison to traditional corollary discharge theory.

claim: The phase of ongoing brain oscillations just prior to stimulus presentation influences its subsequent perception.
source: A recent series of studies has shown that the phase of ongoing brain oscillations just prior to stimulus presentation influences its subsequent perception (Busch et al., 2009; Mathewson et al., 2009; Hanslmayr et al., 2013; Busch and VanRullen, 2010).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Ongoing rhythmic activity is flexible and can be under attentional control.
source: Furthermore, the ongoing rhythmic activity is flexible, can be under attentional control (Landau et al., 2015; Cravo et al., 2013; Samaha et al., 2015; Rohenkohl and Nobre, 2011), and is susceptible to a phase-reset by external events - even of a different modality (Romei et al., 2012; Mercier et al., 2013; Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Ongoing rhythmic activity is susceptible to a phase-reset by external events, even of a different modality.
source: Furthermore, the ongoing rhythmic activity is flexible, can be under attentional control (Landau et al., 2015; Cravo et al., 2013; Samaha et al., 2015; Rohenkohl and Nobre, 2011), and is susceptible to a phase-reset by external events - even of a different modality (Romei et al., 2012; Mercier et al., 2013; Lakatos et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Action planning may be accompanied by an endogenous phase modulation of perceptually-relevant rhythmic activity, resulting in the synchronization of perception and movement initiation.
source: An intriguing possibility is that action planning is accompanied by an endogenous phase modulation of perceptually-relevant rhythmic activity, resulting in the synchronization of perception and movement initiation.
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on prior evidence.

claim: Oscillation-based synchronization would explain the movement-locked fluctuations in visual sensitivity.
source: This oscillation-based synchronization would explain the movement-locked fluctuations in visual sensitivity described above (Tomassini et al., 2015; Benedetto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed to explain prior findings.

claim: Six participants took part in the behavioral experiment.
source: In two experiments, one behavioral and one combined behavioral-EEG, we collected data from six and seventeen participants, respectively, performing the same dual task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Seventeen participants took part in the combined behavioral-EEG experiment.
source: In two experiments, one behavioral and one combined behavioral-EEG, we collected data from six and seventeen participants, respectively, performing the same dual task.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Participants fixated on a central cross that briefly changed color to indicate one of two waiting periods (1.5 or 2.3 s) after which they had to push an isometric joystick with their right hand.
source: Participants fixated on a central cross that briefly changed color to indicate one of two waiting periods (1.5 or 2.3 s) after which they had to push an isometric joystick with their right hand (Figure 1; see also Materials and methods).
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure, illustrated in Figure 1.

claim: Visual performance aligned to movement onset revealed large rhythmic fluctuations, beginning during motor preparation and continuing during motor execution.
source: To investigate the coupling between motor and perceptual processes, we aligned the visual performance (% correct) to movement onset. This revealed large rhythmic fluctuations, beginning during motor preparation and continuing during motor execution (Figure 2a), which confirmed previous findings (Tomassini et al., 2015; Benedetto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2a and citations to prior work.

claim: The rhythmic fluctuations in visual performance aligned to movement onset confirmed previous findings.
source: To investigate the coupling between motor and perceptual processes, we aligned the visual performance (% correct) to movement onset. This revealed large rhythmic fluctuations, beginning during motor preparation and continuing during motor execution (Figure 2a), which confirmed previous findings (Tomassini et al., 2015; Benedetto et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: A prominent theta-band component, centered at ~4 Hz, is present in the perceptual time courses of both the purely behavioral and the combined behavioral-EEG dataset.
source: A prominent theta-band component, centered at ~4 Hz, is present in the perceptual time courses of both the purely behavioral and the combined behavioral-EEG dataset (Figure 2b).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: A second component, in the alpha-band and centered at 10 Hz, is evident only for the purely behavioral dataset.
source: A second component, in the alpha-band and centered at 10 Hz, is evident only for the purely behavioral dataset.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2b.

claim: The alpha-band component may be obscured in the EEG dataset due to the smaller number of trials and the consequent sparser sampling along the time axis.
source: This component may be obscured in the EEG dataset due to the smaller number of trials and the consequent sparser sampling along the time axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on methodological considerations.

claim: Theta oscillations are reliably phase-locked to movement onset.
source: Figure 3d shows that theta oscillations are indeed reliably phase-locked to movement onset.
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: The time course of the theta phase-locking closely matches that of the predictive value of the same oscillatory phase for perception.
source: Crucially, the time course of the theta phase-locking (panel d) closely matches that of the predictive value of the same oscillatory phase for perception (panel a).
evidence: This is supported by comparison of experimental data shown in Figure 3a and 3d.

claim: Theta oscillations are aligned to the future movement very early in time (~−1.4 s).
source: In fact, theta oscillations are aligned to the future movement very early in time (~−1.4 s), phase-alignment then temporarily disappears, and is finally restored before movement initiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Theta phase-alignment temporarily disappears after the early peak and is finally restored before movement initiation.
source: In fact, theta oscillations are aligned to the future movement very early in time (~−1.4 s), phase-alignment then temporarily disappears, and is finally restored before movement initiation.
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Theta oscillations are aligned to the movement with a similar phase angle across participants.
source: Moreover, theta oscillations not only are aligned to the movement but they do so with a similar phase angle across participants.
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: Theta phases that are most predictive for perception are concentrated over frontal electrodes.
source: Figure 3b–e shows the topographies of the early effects (calculated at −1.4 s): theta phases that are most predictive for perception are concentrated over frontal electrodes (panel b, top), and theta phases that are most consistently locked to movement onset are concentrated over more central electrodes (panel e, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3b.

claim: Theta phases that are most consistently locked to movement onset are concentrated over more central electrodes.
source: Figure 3b–e shows the topographies of the early effects (calculated at −1.4 s): theta phases that are most predictive for perception are concentrated over frontal electrodes (panel b, top), and theta phases that are most consistently locked to movement onset are concentrated over more central electrodes (panel e, top).
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3e.

claim: The optimal phase angles and the mean phase angles are nearly identical across the channels.
source: Both the optimal phase angles (i.e., those associated with the highest perceptual performance) and the mean phase angles (expressing the phase relation with movement onset) are nearly identical across the channels (panel b-e, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental EEG data shown in Figure 3b and 3e.

claim: Both the early and the late theta phases independently predict perception.
source: To investigate this, we ran the same logistic regression analysis as used before, but now using as predictors both the early (estimated at −1.4 s) and the late (estimated at −0.1 s) theta phases, allowing their shared explanatory contribution to be discounted. Both the early and the late theta phases retained their original predictive value for perception, with no substantial change in effect size and topography (see Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The early and the late theta phases retaining their predictive value when both are included as predictors is clear evidence for two de-coupled oscillatory phenomena in the theta range.
source: This is clear evidence for two de-coupled oscillatory phenomena in the theta range.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the statistical analysis results.

claim: The early and the late effect have different topographies, with concentration over, respectively, fronto-central and occipito-parietal sites.
source: As an additional piece of evidence, the early and the late effect also have different topographies, with concentration over, respectively, fronto-central and occipito-parietal sites (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The topographic differences, together with the logistic regression analyses, argue for a distinct origin of the early and the late effect.
source: Although this topographic evidence is not conclusive by itself (because of rotating sources and travelling-wave-like phenomena), together with the results of the logistic regression analyses, it argues for a distinct origin of the early and the late effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the combined evidence of topography and statistical analyses.

claim: Both the short and long timing conditions display a similar non-monotonic pattern in the predictive value of the theta phase.
source: To exclude that the early effect is actually induced by the visual cue (rather than being movement-related) and is uniquely present in the short trials, we ran separate analyses for the two timing conditions. Both sets of trials display a similar non-monotonic pattern in the predictive value of the theta phase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The early peak in the theta predictive effect is higher, sharper and earlier for the long as compared to the short trials.
source: Interestingly, the early peak in the effect is higher, sharper and earlier for the long as compared to the short trials.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The temporal dynamics of the theta predictive value is consistently modulated by the motor timing condition.
source: A group-level permutation-based test (with FDR correction across space and time) confirmed that the temporal dynamics of the theta predictive value is consistently modulated by the motor timing condition.
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data.

claim: There is a significant difference between the long and short trials at three different moments in time (−1.475 s, −1/–0.95 s and −0.6 s).
source: Specifically, this statistical analysis revealed a significant difference between the long and short trials at three different moments in time (−1.475 s, −1/–0.95 s and −0.6 s; see Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is supported by statistical analysis of experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The pattern of results clearly rules out any potential confound of the visual cue.
source: This pattern of results clearly rules out any potential confound of the visual cue: (1) the difference in peak latency between the short and long condition (~0.4 s) does not match the difference between the short and the long-time interval (0.8 s), as would be expected if the effect was caused by the visual cue, and (2) the peaks in the predictive value are broader for the short as compared to the long condition, whereas the reverse is expected if the effect is caused by the cue as a result of the larger variability in movement onset times for the long as compared to the short trials (t16 = −4.729, p<0.0001).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data and statistical analysis.

claim: The modulation of the predictive effect by the target movement time (long versus short) suggests that the perceptually relevant theta phases are generated by a process that is involved in movement timing.
source: Thus, the modulation of the predictive effect by the target movement time (long versus short) suggests that the perceptually relevant theta phases are generated by a process that is involved in movement timing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing timing-dependent modulation.

claim: The predictive value calculated using only the pre-stimulus phases closely resembles the one calculated for all trials with respect to temporal profile, topography and optimal phase angle.
source: Figure 4a–b (top) shows that, although slightly weaker (but nevertheless statistically significant at −0.1 s, the time point of the maximum original effect), the predictive value calculated using only the (unconfounded) pre-stimulus phases closely resembles the one calculated for all trials; it does so with respect to temporal profile, topography and optimal phase angle.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: The post-stimulus phases do not contribute significantly to the late effect.
source: We therefore conclude that the post-stimulus phases do not contribute significantly to the late effect, which can hence be considered a genuine predictive effect (like the early effect).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the control analysis showing similar effects with pre-stimulus phases only.

claim: Stimulus-locked phases significantly predict perception, with a steady increase in the predictive power from ~−250 ms until stimulus onset.
source: To investigate this, we calculated the predictive value of the theta phase as a function of stimulus (Gabor) onset time. Stimulus-locked phases (for all as well as for only pre-movement-stimuli, not corrupted by post-movement activity) significantly predict perception, with a steady increase in the predictive power from ~−250 ms until stimulus onset, and same topography and optimal phase as the late movement-locked effect (Figure 4a–b, bottom).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4a-b.

claim: The late movement-locked effect cannot be completely dissociated from the stimulus-locked effect.
source: Thus, contrary to the early predictive effect (~−1.4 s), the late movement-locked effect (from ~−0.5 to 0 s) cannot be completely dissociated from the stimulus-locked effect.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the comparison of movement-locked and stimulus-locked effects.

claim: The results for the movement- and stimulus-locked phases have similar and selective spectro-temporal signatures, with theta-band oscillations showing the highest predictive power, and for the most extended epochs.
source: Figure 4c shows that the results for the movement- (top) and the stimulus-locked (bottom) phases have similar (and selective) spectro-temporal signatures, with theta-band oscillations showing the highest predictive power, and for the most extended epochs.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 4c.

claim: The early effect is proximal to the presentation of the visual stimulus, whereas the late effect foreruns it by more than 1 s.
source: The most striking one is that, whereas the late effect is proximal to the presentation of the visual stimulus, the early effect foreruns it by more than 1 s.
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing temporal differences between early and late effects.

claim: Modulations of behavioral performance by pre-stimulus oscillatory phases have typically been interpreted as reflecting the impact of neuronal excitability at the time of stimulus presentation.
source: Modulations of behavioral performance by pre-stimulus oscillatory phases have typically been interpreted as reflecting the impact of neuronal excitability at the time of stimulus presentation (VanRullen, 2016; Schroeder and Lakatos, 2009; Lakatos et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research and reviews.

claim: Theta phases during preparation for a movement can predict the perceptual outcome long before stimulus appearance and in a way that is independent from the immediate peri-stimulus phase in the same frequency range.
source: Here we report that theta phases during preparation for a movement can predict the perceptual outcome long before stimulus appearance and in a way that is independent from the immediate peri-stimulus phase in the same frequency range (i.e., the late effect).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing independent early and late effects.

claim: Remote oscillatory phases cannot exert any direct influence on sensory processing, at least as would be implied if they reflected different states of neuronal excitability.
source: Clearly, these remote oscillatory phases cannot exert any direct influence on sensory processing, at least as would be implied if they reflected different states of neuronal excitability.
evidence: This is an inference based on the temporal distance between phase estimation and stimulus presentation.

claim: Early theta phases may control a neural switch that brings some sensory area in a self-sustaining state of higher excitability.
source: One possibility is that these early theta phases control a neural switch that brings some sensory area in a self-sustaining state of higher excitability.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Recent studies have described a theta rhythm around 4 Hz in mid- and low-level visual areas (including V1), which is modulated by attention.
source: Interestingly, recent studies have described a theta rhythm around 4 Hz in mid- and low-level visual areas (including V1), which is modulated by attention (Fries et al., 2008; Bosman et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The late effect is susceptible to multiple potential contaminations, which may result in a complex mixture of signals.
source: Finally, it should be noted that, contrary to the early effect, the late effect is susceptible to multiple potential contaminations, which may result in a complex mixture of signals, and in turn produce an effect topography that reflects different sources.
evidence: This is an inference based on methodological considerations.

claim: The current findings are reminiscent of the phase-reset in sensory areas induced by the presentation of external stimuli.
source: The current findings are reminiscent of the phase-reset in sensory areas – often accompanied by periodicity in perceptual performance – induced by the presentation of external stimuli (Romei et al., 2012; Mercier et al., 2013; Landau and Fries, 2012; Fiebelkorn et al., 2013, 2011; Mercier et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison to prior research supported by citations.

claim: In the current study, no external resetting event can be identified.
source: However, in our study, no external resetting event can be identified.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: Both phase-locking and behavioral rhythmicity precede (rather than follow) the event that serves as the temporal reference (i.e., movement onset).
source: In fact, both phase-locking and behavioral rhythmicity precede (rather than follow) the event that serves as the temporal reference (i.e., movement onset).
evidence: This is supported by experimental data showing effects before movement onset.

claim: If any discrete resetting event would play a role, it has to be an endogenous signal (e.g., corollary discharge), operating since the earliest stages of movement planning (>1 s before movement) and carrying an accurate representation of the time of movement initiation.
source: Thus, if any discrete resetting event would play a role here, it has to be an endogenous signal (e.g., corollary discharge), operating since the earliest stages of movement planning (>1 s before movement) and carrying an accurate representation of the time of movement initiation.
evidence: This is a speculative inference based on the temporal characteristics of the observed effects.

claim: Transient theta oscillatory activity could be a constituent part of movement preparation, reflecting the neuronal processes that lead to motor execution.
source: In particular, transient theta oscillatory activity could be a constituent part of movement preparation, reflecting the neuronal processes that lead to motor execution.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: Spontaneous movement initiation (and visual perception) may be influenced by the phase of an ongoing (non-motor) theta rhythm.
source: Alternatively, spontaneous movement initiation (and visual perception) may be influenced by the phase of an ongoing (non-motor) theta rhythm.
evidence: This is a speculative alternative explanation proposed by the authors.

claim: The fact that the movement timing condition (short/long) modulates the temporal dynamics of the predictive effect in a non-trivial way suggests that the identified theta rhythm might be involved in the planning of the movement, at least with respect to its timing component.
source: However, the fact that the movement timing condition (short/long) modulates the temporal dynamics of the predictive effect in a non-trivial way (i.e., not accounted for by the visual cue) suggests that the identified theta rhythm might indeed be involved in the planning of the movement, at least with respect to its timing component.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing timing-dependent modulation.

claim: Previous work has proposed that the motor system can improve the temporal tuning of attentional fluctuations, optimizing information selection when sensory events are rhythmic or temporally predictable.
source: Previous work has proposed that the motor system can improve the temporal tuning of attentional fluctuations, optimizing information selection when sensory events are rhythmic or, at least, temporally predictable (Morillon et al., 2015; Arnal, 2012; Saleh et al., 2010; Arnal and Giraud, 2012; Morillon et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: In the current study, temporal attention cannot play a role, because the visual stimuli are unpredictable.
source: However, in our study, temporal attention cannot play a role, because the visual stimuli are unpredictable.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experimental design.

claim: An endogenous 4 Hz theta rhythm synchronizes perception and action in the absence of any overt rhythmicity either in motor behavior or in external sensory events.
source: The present study shows that an endogenous 4 Hz theta rhythm synchronizes perception and action in the absence of any overt rhythmicity either in motor behavior or in external sensory events.
evidence: This is the main conclusion drawn from the experimental data.

claim: The potential involvement of theta oscillations in sensorimotor processing has been postulated before.
source: The potential involvement of theta oscillations in sensorimotor processing has been postulated before (Bland and Oddie, 2001; Caplan et al., 2003) but no compelling neurophysiological evidence had been provided so far.
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: The pattern in the data suggests the existence of two very weakly coupled ~4 Hz oscillations, an early one and a late one, of which the first is likely to be involved in motor timing.
source: The pattern in the data suggests the existence of two very weakly coupled ~4 Hz oscillations, an early one and a late one, of which the first is likely to be involved in motor timing.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental data showing two independent effects.

claim: Neuronal oscillations in the theta-band may be instrumental in binding action and perception at early stages, possibly providing a common temporal reference frame for integrating sensory information with the emerging motor intention.
source: These neuronal oscillations in the theta-band may be instrumental in binding action and perception at early stages, possibly providing a common temporal reference frame for integrating sensory information with the emerging motor intention.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the experimental findings.

claim: Eighteen healthy participants (11 females; age 24 ± 4.3 year, MEAN±SD) took part in the combined behavioral-EEG experiment.
source: Eighteen healthy participants (11 females; age 24 ± 4.3 year, MEAN±SD), took part in the combined behavioral-EEG experiment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: One participant (female) withdrew before completing the experiment and was excluded from the analysis due to insufficient data.
source: One participant (female) withdrew before completing the experiment and was excluded from the analysis due to insufficient data.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design and data exclusion.

claim: The study and experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethical Review Board (Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Social Sciences, Radboud University, The Netherlands).
source: The study and experimental procedures were approved by the local Ethical Review Board (Ethics Committee of the Faculty of Social Sciences, Radboud University, The Netherlands).
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical approval.

claim: Participants provided written, informed consent after explanation of the task and experimental procedures, in accordance with the guidelines of the local Ethical Review Board.
source: Participants provided written, informed consent after explanation of the task and experimental procedures, in accordance with the guidelines of the local Ethical Review Board.
evidence: This is a direct statement about ethical procedures.
